stem:
Draw both chair conformations. Circle the more stable one, or say that they are equal. What is the relationship between the two chairs?
[[ring:1u:CH3,2u:CH(CH3)2]]

steps.h: Methyl is on a wedge (up) and isopropyl is on a wedge (up), on carbons 1 and 2. Same face: cis-1,2.

ask.q: Are the two groups on the same face of the ring?

steps.h:
Put each group on its carbon, up or down as in the flat drawing, then flip the ring: axial and equatorial swap, up and down do not. No wedges on a chair. First chair: C1 methyl axial, C2 isopropyl equatorial. After the flip: C1 methyl equatorial, C2 isopropyl axial.
[[chair:1u:CH3,2u:CH(CH3)2|A]]
[[chair:1u:CH3,2u:CH(CH3)2|B]]

Each chair has one axial group, but not the same one. Axial methyl costs 1.74 kcal/mol (Table 5.3). Axial isopropyl costs 2.61 kcal/mol (Table 5.3). Circle the chair with the larger group, isopropyl, equatorial: it is better by 0.87 kcal/mol.

ask.q: Which group costs more when it is axial?
ask.a: Isopropyl. So the better chair has it equatorial.

steps.h: In one chair methyl is axial, in the other isopropyl is axial. These shapes cannot be laid on top of each other and they are not mirror images. They are diastereomers. Quick test: chairs with different energies can only be diastereomers, because identical shapes and mirror images always have the same energy.

ask.q: Can the flipped chair be laid exactly on the first one? If not, is it the mirror image?
ask.a: Neither. Different energies already rule both out: diastereomers.

solution.answer: The chair with isopropyl equatorial (and methyl axial) is more stable. The two chairs are diastereomers.
solution.rule: Chairs of different energy are diastereomers. Larger group equatorial; both equatorial beats both axial.

stem:
Draw both chair conformations. Circle the more stable one, or say that they are equal. What is the relationship between the two chairs?
[[ring:1d:Cl,2d:Cl]]

steps.h: The two Cl groups are on a dash (down) and a dash (down), on carbons 1 and 2. Same face: cis-1,2.

ask.q: Are the two groups on the same face of the ring?

steps.h:
Put each group on its carbon, up or down as in the flat drawing, then flip the ring: axial and equatorial swap, up and down do not. No wedges on a chair. First chair: C1 Cl equatorial, C2 Cl axial. After the flip: C1 Cl axial, C2 Cl equatorial.
[[chair:1d:Cl,2d:Cl|A]]
[[chair:1d:Cl,2d:Cl|B]]

Each chair has exactly one axial Cl and one equatorial Cl. Same cost in both (about 0.53 kcal/mol (a literature value: the lecture table lists only alkyl groups)): equal in energy, K = 1. Circle neither.

ask.q: How many axial groups does each chair have?
ask.a: One each, and it is the same group. The energies are equal.

steps.h: Equal energy means the chairs are either the same or mirror images, so test it. Try to lay the flipped chair on the first one: it does not fit, however it is turned. But the mirror image of the first chair is exactly the flipped chair. Non-superimposable mirror images are enantiomers. The lecture calls them conformational enantiomers. They interconvert by the ring flip, which is why the molecule as a whole is achiral.

ask.q: Can the flipped chair be laid exactly on the first one? If not, is it the mirror image?
ask.a: It cannot be superimposed, but it is the mirror image: enantiomers.

solution.answer: The two chairs are equal in energy. The two chairs are enantiomers.
solution.rule: cis-1,2 with identical groups: equal energy, mirror-image chairs (enantiomers).
